newsitem.title: UK: P&o shipping overhaul to hold back 97 results.
newsitem.headline: P&o shipping overhaul to hold back 97 results.

text.p: The Peninsular & Oriental Steam Navigation Co (P&O) warned on Tuesday that restrucuturing of its container shipping and ferries businesses would hold back group results for 1997.
"Underlying profitability is set to improve sharply although restructuring in Containers and Ferries will constrain the 1997 results," chairman Lord Sterling said in his results statement for 1996.
The warning came with the shipping to construction and property group's announcement of 1996 results.

It reported a marginal increase in profits last year, to 320.4 million pounds ($517.9 million) from 320.1 million pounds in 1995, but exceptional gains from disposals boosted the pretax result to 332.8 million pounds, against 320.4 million in 1995, on sales up 519 million pounds at 7.09 billion pounds.

Sterling said the merging of its containers and ferries businesses with European rivals would reap benefits in 1998, but the current year's results were likely to be hit by the costs of rationalisation, involving redundancies.
"The full impact of the measures we are taking will start to come through strongly in 1998," he said.
P&O has just merged its container shipping business with that of Dutch group Koninklijke Nedlloyd Groep NV.
"P&O Nedlloyd Container Line has already made considerable progress towards achieving annual cost savings of at least $200 million and a full year's savings will be realised in 1998," Sterling said.
He told Reuters in a post-results interview that the rationalisation costs would probably run at around $100 million in the current year, with 50 percent due to P&O.

Meanwhile P&O has also agreed to join forces with Swedish rival Stena Line AB in the English Channel ferries business to combat the new competition from the Channel Tunnel railway which has captured 40 percent of the main Dover-Calais route.

That deal is still waiting on the outcome of an investigation by the British competition authorities and a decision is not now expected before the May election, but Sterling said rationalisation work would be rapid if it got the go ahead. "We are all ready to go," he told Reuters.
